title: I Used the Community-Sailing Tiller Checkout on the Skipper Who Skipped the Log

parts.text: I stepped onto dinghy four at 10:06 a.m. and skipper Rourke was already holding our numbered tiller. The board said: ONE BOAT. THREE HOURS. TILLER FOLLOWS THE LOG. I was forty, club member, holding a float plan that listed our bay. Rourke shrugged. "Skippers are the boat." I photographed the board, the log, and his hand on our tiller. Then I asked for the checkout sheet. At 10:14 the dock pinged why Rourke's name was not on our dinghy. I kept my voice dock-quiet and let the timestamp talk. A board is only a board until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The dock can see Rourke's hand on our tiller during our checkout.

social.video_title: He held our numbered tiller without the log — Part 1/2
social.description: Dinghy dock, a skipper on our tiller, a three-hour log he skipped. I logged the hand. Would you have asked for the checkout sheet?

parts.text: Rourke called it a hold until the dock asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the hand still. The tiller went back to our clip. Rourke ran his own three hours and told the next skipper atmosphere was always about wind. Wind is a word skippers use when a log exists. Boat policy now has a second line: SKIPPERS ARE NOT THE BOAT. I keep our tiller on a labeled hook. Rourke brown-bags his jokes. The dock finally looks like a checkout, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Skippers are not the boat — Part 2/2
social.description: Checkout sheet, numbered tiller, and a second line on the board. Was a hold ever our dinghy?
